title: Benzene + toluene, 10 stages, saturated-liquid feed: the worked example of The ChemSep Book, section 1.2
purpose: The complete benchmark of milestone M2a: a real column from an open source with published stage results. Kooijman and Taylor, The ChemSep Book, 2nd edition (2006, public domain), section 1.2 'Distillation of Benzene and Toluene' (pp. 9-17) and its results in section 1.3 (pp. 18-20): Figure 1.18 (balances), Figure 1.19 (T/P/flow profiles), Figure 1.20 (benzene's liquid and vapour mole fractions and K-values), Figure 1.21 (stream table). The engine is compared twice: numerically with reference_mesh.py on CHEPTA's own method (tight tolerances), and with the published numbers, which come from another property method (agreement tolerances, kept apart).

source.citation: H.A. Kooijman, R. Taylor, The ChemSep Book, 2nd edition, 2006, section 1.2 (pp. 9-17) and section 1.3 (pp. 18-20)
source.access: Public domain ('This publication is public domain', p. 2 of the PDF); read 2026-10-29
source.tables: Figures 1.18, 1.19, 1.20 and 1.21 (screenshots of ChemSep's result tables; the numbers are read off the images, which are sharp text, not graphs)

method_choice: docs/METHOD_SELECTION.md rules 2 and 6: benzene and toluene are nonpolar hydrocarbons, so Peng-Robinson for both phases (the maintainer, 2026-10-29), at any reduced temperature (here 0.62 to 0.67 by Kay's rule). Its Peng-Robinson k_ij is fitted to the isobaric T-x-y data of Li et al. (2014) in the NIST TRC ThermoML Archive (k_ij = -0.0003, 2026-10-29; validation/python/eos_fit_kij.py); until then the databank had none and k_ij = 0 was used, with a warning. The published example uses an activity model instead, K = gamma p*/P with UNIFAC and ChemSep's Antoine equations and constant molar overflow (p. 13); the pair is nearly ideal (infinite-dilution activity coefficients about 0.98 with NRTL), so the method matters little (METHOD_SELECTION.md, rule 6).

setup_from_source.pressure: 1.1 atm in every stage and the condenser, no pressure drop (pp. 14-15); ChemSep shows 1.11458 bar. 1.1 x 101.325 kPa = 111.4575 kPa
setup_from_source.feed: saturated liquid (vapour fraction 0) at the column pressure, equimolar, 1 kg/s 'corresponds to 11.7471 mol/s' (p. 14); on stage 5 of 10 (p. 11)
setup_from_source.column: simple distillation, total condenser, partial reboiler, 10 stages counted with both (the condenser is stage 1, the reboiler stage 10: Figure 1.19), Murphree efficiency 1, no heat loss (p. 16)
setup_from_source.specifications: reflux ratio 2 and bottoms flow 5.874 mol/s (p. 17)
setup_from_source.property_method_of_the_source: DECHEMA K-model (K = gamma p*/P), UNIFAC activity coefficients, Antoine vapour pressures from ChemSep's databank, enthalpy model 'none' (constant molar overflow) (p. 13); solved to ChemSep's default accuracy of 1e-3 (p. 18)

published.units: T in degC, flows in mol/s, mole fractions of benzene

where.T_C, L_mol_s, V_mol_s, reflux_ratio, boi: Figure 1.19 (p. 19); L of stage 10 is shown as 'BR=2.99954', V of stage 1 as 'RR=2'
where.x_benzene, y_benzene, K_benzene: Figure 1.20 (p. 20); y of stage 1 (0.97095) is the vapour in equilibrium with the condenser's liquid, not a stream: the condenser is total

published.text: p. 19: the temperatures 'vary from 85 degC in the condenser to 111 degC in the reboiler'; p. 20: benzene 'condensing at 92 mole%'; p. 23: the relative volatility 'varies from 2.25 in the reboiler to 2.6 in the condenser'; p. 24: the vapour flows are constant and the liquid flows jump at the feed stage (constant molar overflow)
published.notes: The K column of Figure 1.20 is not y/x of the same figure: y/x is 0.03 % to 2.8 % below it, most at the top (stage 1: y/x = 1.0491, K = 1.07974). The x and y columns are consistent with the flows of Figure 1.19 through the operating lines (test/benchmark-columns.test.js), so x, y, T and the flows are compared and the K column is shown only.

behaviour: the engine, on CHEPTA's method (Peng-Robinson for both phases, k_ij = 0, energy balances), matches reference_mesh.py within the numerical tolerances
the engine's profile agrees with the published one within the agreement tolerances (agreement_with_published_example)
the molar flows are nearly, not exactly, constant: CHEPTA solves energy balances where the published example assumes constant molar overflow
expected.branch: One solution expected (a near-ideal binary with reflux-ratio and bottoms-flow specifications): the reference's solution is the one to match.
qualifications: the Peng-Robinson pair benzene + toluene uses its k_ij fitted to the ThermoML data of Li et al. (2014), tier fitted, shown in the result's qualifications (until 2026-10-29: k_ij = 0, with a warning)

engine_against_reference.why: Proposal 0015, Engineering basis: flows within 1e-6 relative of the independent MESH solution. Both solve the same equations to residuals of 1e-8 or less, so the difference is the solvers' convergence only.

balances_on_every_stage.why: Proposal 0015: every stage's balances closed to 1e-8. Material: |residual| / F; energy: |residual| / (F x 10 kJ/mol); summation and equilibrium are mole fractions.

agreement_with_published_example.applies_to: T and the benzene mole fraction x of each of the ten stages, and x_D and x_B
agreement_with_published_example.why: The published numbers come from another property method (UNIFAC and ChemSep's Antoine equations, constant molar overflow) solved to a norm of 1e-3, so they are not a numerical reference. CHEPTA's method (Peng-Robinson, k_ij = 0) gives, in reference_mesh.py, at most 0.85 K and 0.018 from them (0.73 K and 0.013 with constant molar overflow; fixture checks.published); NRTL with the ChemSep set gave 0.37 K and 0.0059. The tolerances, chosen by W7 after that comparison for the maintainer to confirm, are a little above the Peng-Robinson differences, so a change in CHEPTA's records or in the engine that moves the column more is seen. They state agreement between two property methods, not the accuracy of either against measured data.
